en: Composed by the Silla śramaṇa Yiji:

An Exposition of the Forty-eight Minor Precepts on the Precept of Gathering Wholesome Dharmas (Śubha-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla). The exposition of the forty-eight minor precepts is also divided into three major sections: first, the introductory summary; second, the sequential detailed explanation;
and third, the concluding summary upon completion of the discourse. Within the detailed explanation, the forty-eight minor precepts follow the sequence of the text. [End of fragment]
The *jié* (concluding sections) consist of five parts in total;
at the end of each section, there is a reference to other texts.
There should be an extensive explanation.
Within these five sections, each passage taken individually applies to all three aggregates (*tri-skandha*).
In every section, the meaning of abandoning evil, embracing the good, and benefiting sentient beings is explained.
Therefore, following the *Zongdu lun* (Compendium of Doctrines),
the first ten grave precepts (*śīla*) are classified as the code of discipline (*vinaya*),
while the subsequent forty-eight items are categorized as the remaining two [categories].
The Sūtra explains that the precept of restraining oneself consists of the ten *pārājikas*;
the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas consists of the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates;
and the precept of benefiting sentient beings consists of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
The transformation reaches all sentient beings,
and all sentient beings attain peace and happiness.
Furthermore, within the forty-eight [vows]:
Of the first thirty precepts, most are for the purpose of gathering wholesome qualities;
of the latter eighteen precepts, most are for the purpose of benefiting sentient beings.
Among the forty-four minor precepts in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, [the same distinction applies].
The first thirty-three also serve to encompass wholesome qualities,
while the latter eleven precepts are for the benefit of sentient beings;
thus, although these precepts appear and disappear relative to one another, their essential characteristics remain.
The classification of the characteristics of the entire school is also similar [to that of other schools].
Furthermore, the Sūtras establish the fundamental teachings,
while the Śāstras determine the categories of their meaning.
Therefore, the Sūtra and the Śāstra must not contradict one another.
Within the Śāstra’s exposition of the nine aspects of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*),
the second is "all-encompassing ethical discipline" (*sarva-śīla*).
That is to say, the precepts pertaining to the household life and the precepts pertaining to the homeless life;
these are called all precepts.
Furthermore, based on these two categories, pure ethical discipline is briefly explained as being of three types.
First, the ethical discipline of restraint;
second, the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas;
third, the ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings.
Regarding the vow of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*):
it refers to the sevenfold Pratimokṣa vows undertaken by bodhisattvas, which range from the bhikṣu vows down to the upāsikā vows;
these seven types rely upon both the lay and monastic divisions.
It should be understood that this is called the bodhisattva’s morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*).
As for the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*),
it refers to the various bodhisattvas who, having received the morality of restraint...
Thereafter, all that is accumulated as wholesome through body,
speech, and mind for the sake of great enlightenment is collectively termed the "precept of gathering virtuous dharmas" (kuśaladharmasaṃgrāhaka-śīla).
What does this mean? It refers to bodhisattvas who, relying upon and abiding in the precepts,
[apply themselves] to hearing, reflection, and the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
He diligently applies himself to training while delighting in solitary dwellings.
Thus, from time to time, he diligently practices the acts of joining his palms, rising to welcome,
inquiring after their well-being, prostrating, and showing reverence toward his elders and superiors.
He diligently cultivates respectful service toward his elders;
he compassionately and earnestly attends to and provides for those who are ill;
and he bestows praise upon all sublime teachings.
One sincerely praises individuals who possess virtuous qualities;
and regarding all the meritorious deeds of all sentient beings throughout the realms of the ten directions,
one expresses sympathetic joy by speaking with a superior intention and pure faith.
One should contemplate and cultivate patience regarding all transgressions committed by others;
and one should dedicate all roots of virtue— whether already performed or yet to be performed by means of body, speech, and mind—
toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
From time to time, one should give rise to various right aspirations;
one should make offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha with all kinds of supreme and exquisite requisites;
and one should constantly and vigorously cultivate all categories of wholesome qualities with diligent effort.
Abiding in heedfulness regarding body, speech, and mind;
correctly mindful, clearly comprehending, and practicing rightly within the various training rules (śikṣāpada); guarding and closely protecting the doors of the sense faculties;
and knowing moderation in food.
One should constantly practice during both the first and last watches of the night;
remain awake, draw near to virtuous persons, and rely upon spiritual friends.
One should examine one's own transgressions with precision, clearly understanding them and perceiving their faults deeply.
Having thoroughly examined and understood these deep faults,
those who have not yet committed them should focus their minds on guarding against them;
those who have already committed them should, with a sincere heart, confess before the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and fellow practitioners, and repent according to the Dharma so as to eliminate them.

All such categories of ethical discipline that attract, sustain, and increase all wholesome dharmas are called the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline of gathering virtuous qualities (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).
What is the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*)?
It should be known that this consists briefly of eleven aspects.
What are these eleven? They are as follows:
when bodhisattvas are able to bring about the welfare and benefit of sentient beings.
He acts as a companion in various undertakings;
furthermore, he acts as a companion in attending to sentient beings by caring for them when illnesses and other forms of suffering arise.
Furthermore, by relying on various mundane and supramundane benefits, bodhisattvas are able to expound essential teachings for sentient beings;
they first teach through skillful means and first teach in accordance with reason.
Subsequently, he causes those beings to obtain their respective benefits and purposes.
Furthermore, regarding sentient beings who have previously rendered him kindness, the bodhisattva maintains a virtuous sense of gratitude and repays them in person according to what is appropriate.
Furthermore, regarding sentient beings who have fallen into various fears— such as those caused by lions, tigers, wolves, malevolent spirits, kings, thieves, water, or fire—
all bodhisattvas are able to protect and rescue them, causing them to leave such states of terror behind.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas skillfully console those sentient beings who have suffered the loss of wealth, treasures, or relatives, causing them to be free from sorrow and grief.
Moreover, bodhisattvas [act] toward those sentient beings who are destitute of the various necessities of life.
He bestows all requisites for life;
furthermore, the bodhisattvas, in accordance with reason,
provide proper support and guide the community in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas conform to the world by engaging in worldly affairs,
speech, summoning, coming and going, conversation, and expressions of congratulation and consolation,
attending to them as they arise at the appropriate time.
Receiving food, drink, and other such things from others—
in short, one should distance oneself from all of these.
They are able to manifest that which is unbeneficial and contrary to their intentions,
while their minds remain compliant toward all other matters.
Furthermore, whether in private or in public, these bodhisattvas reveal all their genuine virtues.
They cause all sentient beings to rejoice and advance in their learning.
Furthermore, toward those who have transgressed,
Bodhisattvas inwardly maintain a superior intention of intimacy, seeking their benefit and happiness.
They subdue, reprimand, punish, and expel them,
desiring to lead them out of unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas employ the skillful means of supernormal powers.
He manifests the various appearances of the realms of existence, such as the hells and so forth,
causing sentient beings to feel weary of and detached from unwholesome states;

through skillful means, he leads them to enter the Buddha’s holy teaching, inspiring joy, faith, and delight, and giving rise to a sense of wonder so that they may diligently practice the correct path.
Now, upon examining the forty-eight minor precepts,
it is evident that the texts differ in their mutual inclusion or omission and in their expansion or contraction compared to what is stated in the treatise;
there are also differences in their sequence and order.
The sūtras establish the basis of the teaching by setting it forth separately according to specific matters;
the śāstras analyze the categories of meaning by explaining them collectively according to their types.
In establishing the meanings through expansion or condensation, one must exercise careful discernment.
1. The First Precept of the Ten Precepts: Reverencing and Serving One’s Elders. The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha, when one is about to receive the position of a king..."
When assuming the rank of a Wheel-Turning King,
or when officials receive their positions,
one should first receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
All ghosts and spirits shall protect the person of the King and the persons of his hundred officials;
all Buddhas shall rejoice.
Having thus received the precepts, [they are established].
One should give rise to a mind of filial piety and respect toward one's seniors,
preceptors (upādhyāya), ācāryas, and those who are fellow students, share the same views, and practice the same path.
One should rise to welcome, prostrate, and inquire after their well-being;
yet the bodhisattva, on the contrary, gives rise to arrogance, pride, delusion, and anger,
and fails to rise to welcome, prostrate, or inquire after their well-being.

If one does not provide each with offerings in accordance with the Dharma—supplying them by selling one's own body, kingdom, city, sons, daughters, the seven treasures, and all manner of goods—one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

As stated in the treatise: at such times, one should diligently cultivate toward all elders and superiors the practices of joining the palms, rising to welcome them, inquiring after their well-being, prostrating, and showing reverence.
One should therefore diligently practice respectful service toward one's elders and superiors.
For one who wishes to gather wholesome qualities must rely upon superior conditions;
if one is arrogant toward those worthy of honor, it will obstruct progress in virtue.
Therefore, the precept was established to ensure respectful service.
Although the principles for the full completion of an offense should be discussed in detail, since this is not a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*),
it does not necessarily require all five conditions to be met.
Therefore, among the minor defilements (*āpatti*), the conditions for transgression are presented in brief.

Nevertheless, within the five conditions— namely, the object, perception, intention, application, and completion— although these are not natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) or courses of action (*karmapatha*), [they still constitute transgressions].
It must necessarily be possessed.

Regarding the fourth category of afflictions, they exist both in cases of defiled transgressions and in cases of non-defiled transgressions; however, they are not necessarily present within the latter.
Regarding the gravity of the offenses incurred through the formation of fetters: those committed intentionally and with defilement are all grave;
those not committed intentionally and without defilement are all light.
All the precepts are likewise;
they need not be discussed further.
As for the similarities and differences among the training rules (śikṣāpada):
Both the great and the small [vehicles] prohibit it;
however, for the Śrāvakas, it is prohibited within the framework of avoiding faults,
whereas for Bodhisattvas, it is prohibited within the framework of gathering wholesome qualities.
The seven classes of followers commit this offense equally.
Regarding the fifth of the twenty-eight minor precepts for lay practitioners, it says:
"If an upāsaka, having received and upheld the precepts..."
If one sees a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, an elder, a senior, or various upāsakas and fails to rise to greet them,
welcome them, or inquire after their well-being,
that upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence.
There is no arising of falling into impurity through intentional action.
In the text, each precept consists of three parts:
the identification of the person, the introduction of the matter, and the formulation of the offense.
Regarding the sequence of matters,
the various precepts differ in their degree of gravity;
this precept has three [levels].
First, an exhortation to receive the precepts;
second, clarifying that one should show respect;
third, clarifying that violating these constitutes an offense.
In the initial exhortation to receive [the precepts], three categories are generally cited.
The first two apply exclusively to laypeople;
the third applies to both monastics and laity alike.
A renunciant bodhisattva may also be eligible to serve as a *saṃghasthavira* (monastic head) and so forth; therefore,
although such roles are prohibited by the sūtras, the positions of *saṃghasthavira* and others are nonetheless established.
I shall certainly not be able to resist;
there must be a reason for this matter.
I fear it concerns those in high positions.
Because one has indulged in unrestrained and improper conduct, this precept is established to restrain them and prevent arrogance and luxury.
If one can accept it and practice accordingly, then the spirits and Buddhas will rejoice and protect them;
they will be able to secure their own well-being in the near term and cause the Dharma to flourish in the distant future.
Therefore, one should be encouraged to receive the precepts;
even if they have previously received them, they should receive them again when facing the actual situation,
out of a desire to show respect for the matter.
The passage from "having already obtained" onwards clarifies that one should show reverence.
As for the "mind of filial piety and obedience," it means following their instructions and training without daring to contravene them.
"One with a respectful mind" means one who reveres that person's virtuous conduct and does not dare to be arrogant toward them.
"Elder" (upādhyāya) means...
There is no one above him, thus he is the "upper seat" (upādhyāya).
"Upādhyāya" is a corruption of this sound;
if it were to be rendered correctly, it should be "upādhyāya."
This is further called the "Preceptor" (upādhyāya),
which refers to the one from whom one receives the precepts. As for the "Ācārya":
If one were to speak correctly, it should be called *ācārya*,
which here means "preceptor" (*kǐfàn*).
There are five kinds of this.
First, shaving the hair;
second, leaving the household life;
third, instruction.
The four *karmas*,
the five dependencies,
and those who are great companions in study, view, and practice.
This refers to fellow students who are senior in age.
Furthermore, it refers to those who study the Great Dharma together, practice the Great View together, and cultivate the Great Conduct together.
To oppose them constitutes a middling offense.
As for those who instead give rise to conceit, arrogance, and delusion:
they are conceited because they are not filial and submissive;
they are arrogant because they do not show respect.
Not knowing where one ought to show respect is precisely the mind of delusion. To emphasize this grave admonition,
the text uses the example of selling one's own body as an illustration.
One should even be prepared to sacrifice one's own body;
how much more so should one not fail to pay homage?
The third precept among the forty-four states:
If bodhisattvas, while dwelling in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline,
see elders, virtuous persons worthy of respect, or fellow practitioners of the Dharma approaching,
yet are constrained by pride and harbor a mind of resentment or a mind of malice;

He does not rise to welcome others nor offer them a superior seat; when others come to converse, discuss, offer greetings, or inquire after him, he is constrained by pride and harbors a mind of resentment and a mind of malice.
To respond with speech that does not accord with correct reasoning is called an offense;
such a transgression constitutes an afflicted offense.
It is not due to arrogance, nor is it constrained by a mind of resentment or a mind of malice;
rather, it arises solely from a mind of indolence, laziness, forgetfulness, or moral neutrality.
This is called an offense.
If there is a transgression that is not a defiled offense,
it constitutes no offense in the following cases: namely, when one is afflicted by a serious illness.
Whether one’s mind is deranged or one is asleep, another person may,
perceiving them to be awake, approach and engage in conversation, greeting, consolation, and inquiry.
Either he himself proclaims, teaches, discusses, or provides definitive analysis for others;
or he engages in conversation and offers greetings with others;
or he lends an attentive ear while others teach, discuss, or provide definitive analysis.
Or there may be those who violate those who preach the true Dharma; [in such cases],
it is for the sake of protecting the mind of the Dharma-preacher,
or for the sake of employing skillful means to discipline and subdue them, leading them out of unwholesome states and establishing them in wholesome states.
Either to protect the monastic regulations,
or out of consideration for the minds of many sentient beings,
one does not respond.

In all these cases, there is no transgression. **The Second Precept: Not Drinking Alcohol** If a Buddha’s disciple intentionally drinks alcohol, the faults of such drinking are immeasurable. If one passes a vessel of alcohol from their own hand to another person to drink, they shall be without hands for five hundred lifetimes; how much more so if they drink it themselves! One must not teach any person or any sentient being to drink alcohol, let alone drink it oneself. No kind of alcohol whatsoever may be drunk. If one intentionally drinks it oneself or teaches others to drink it, one commits a minor offense (light defilement). Alcohol is the source of heedlessness.
It is established because it can produce various transgressions and oppose all wholesome dharmas.
It is equally prohibited for the seven classes of followers in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Among the twenty-eight rules, the second precept states:
If an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, indulges in the pleasure of drinking alcohol, he incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
This is the third of the introductory matters;
first, it reveals the fault.
Second, one must not instruct others [to drink], as it is prohibited by the rules;
third, if one intentionally drinks for oneself, one violates the rule and incurs an offense.
The first point clarifies the loss [of the precept].
Therefore, for one who drinks alcohol, it is as if the prohibition against drinking were being violated;
furthermore, according to the Vinaya, even if one perceives what is not alcohol as alcohol, one still commits an offense.
If from beginning to end one has no intention to drink alcohol,
and by mistake or delusion merely thinks one is drinking water,
it is reasonable that this should be permitted.
If one originally has the intention to drink alcohol,
even if at the time of drinking one claims it is not alcohol,
one should still be considered to have committed an offense.
Regarding the statement that "the faults of alcohol give rise to immeasurable sins":
although it is not inherently evil, it can trigger inherent evil; therefore, it is said that its faults are immeasurable.
As stated in the treatise:
When one is intoxicated by alcohol, there is no evil deed that will not be committed, with the sole exception of the matter of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* fully elucidates thirty-six faults,
while the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* lists ten kinds of transgressions.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"There are ten faults for anyone who drinks alcohol.
The first is that one's complexion becomes ugly."
Second, inferior strength;
third, unclear vision;
fourth, manifesting signs of anger.
Fifth, it ruins fields, occupations, and the means of livelihood.
Sixth, it increases and brings about illness.
Seventh, it augments strife and litigation.
Eighth, one lacks renown and ill repute spreads.
Ninth, wisdom diminishes.
Tenth, at the dissolution of the body after death, one falls into the evil realms.
These are called the ten faults.
From this day forward, those who follow me as their teacher must not even place the tip of a blade of grass or wood into wine and drink it.
As for "passing over a vessel," it means crossing over a vessel containing wine.
One said, "Take a vessel of wine and give it to him to drink.
Another said, "..."
One merely passes an empty vessel to them to pour [the drink] into;
the former [case] refers to sending another to drink,
while the latter refers to instructing another to drink.
The meaning is entirely without error.
Regarding "five hundred lifetimes without hands":
this refers to having held a vessel for wine in one's hand in a previous life, and thus receiving the retribution of being without hands.
Such as the class of creatures like earthworms;
or else, even if born among humans, one may be born without hands. Some say:
There are five periods of five hundred years each:
the first five hundred years are spent in the Salt-Brine Hell,
and the second five hundred years are spent amidst boiling urine.
Three hundred and fifty become dung-worms;
four hundred and fifty become flies and moths;
five hundred become humans who are dull-witted and ignorant.
What is now said as "five hundred" may perhaps be the final [limit].
The regulation should not be applied in the interim. One must not teach all people to drink.
This means that one must not instruct others to drink,
nor cause any sentient being to drink alcohol;
that is to say, one must not send it to others for them to drink.
How much more so for one who drinks alcohol oneself;
it is in order to prevent the fault of one's own negligence that the other case is cited by way of analogy to oneself.
The Vinaya states:
"As for 'liquor,' it refers to liquor made from wood, liquor made from non-glutinous rice, liquor made from other types of rice, and liquor made from barley."
If there is any other substance made into liquor according to the methods for making liquor,
or if it is mixed liquor—
possessing the color, fragrance, and taste of liquor— it should not be drunk.
There may be alcohol that lacks the color, aroma, and taste of alcohol, yet it should not be drunk;
there may be alcohol that lacks the color, aroma, and taste of alcohol, yet it should not be drunk;
there may be alcohol that lacks the color, aroma, and taste of alcohol, yet it should not be drunk.
One should not drink that which is not wine but possesses the color, fragrance, and taste of wine;
as explained at length therein.
There is no offense [in the following cases]:
If one has such an illness that it cannot be cured by other medicines,
one should take alcohol as medicine.
If one applies wine to a wound, there is no offense whatsoever. **The Third Precept:

The Prohibition Against Eating Meat** O Disciples of the Buddha, if you intentionally eat meat, you must not eat any kind of meat. Those who eat meat sever the seeds of great compassion and the Buddha-nature; all sentient beings will see them and depart. Therefore, no Bodhisattva may eat the flesh of any living being. To eat the flesh of sentient beings is to incur immeasurable sin. If one intentionally eats it, they commit a minor transgression. This precept was established because eating meat severs the seed of great compassion.
For śrāvakas, prior to their attainment of nirvāṇa, three types of purity were permitted while the rest were not;
after attaining nirvāṇa, none were permitted. For bodhisattvas, none were permitted at any time, whether before or after [attaining realization].
The precept is established for all seven classes of followers.
In the textual sequence of the matter, it first clarifies the fault,
and subsequently prescribes that one should not eat [the forbidden food].
If one later violates this, an offense is committed.
Regarding the prohibition against eating all meat:
whether it is pure or impure, none may be eaten.
Regarding those who sever the seeds of great compassion and the Buddha-nature,
as the sutra says:
"Because there are people who eat [flesh], they kill."
Because one eats with such awareness, one cuts off the seeds of compassion.
As for all sentient beings seeing [the practitioner] and departing:
it is like a bird that feels trembling fear even upon entering the shadow of Śāriputra.
If this is the case for those who possess residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*),
how much more so for those who have not entirely severed the three poisons?
To eat meat incurs immeasurable transgressions.
From eating [forbidden foods] up to killing, one incurs immeasurable offenses.

**The Fourth Precept: Not Eating Pungent Vegetables.** If a Buddha’s disciple does not eat the five pungent vegetables—garlic (*laśuna*), leeks (*gṛñjana*), scallions (*palāṇḍu*), onions (*bhallātaka*), and *hiṅgu* (asafoetida)—among all types of food, these five kinds must not be eaten. If one intentionally eats them, they constitute a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*). They are prohibited because their foul odor obstructs pure dharmas.
The prohibitions for both the great and the small are the same for all seven classes of followers;
according to the Vinaya,
the rules for women should be somewhat more stringent.
Because they produce flowers and have color.
As for *gecong*, *tucong*, and *lancong*,
there are no *xiè* (garlic) or *jiǔ* (leeks) among them.
However, the onion is divided into three;
the distinct characteristics of these three are difficult to discern. Some say:
*Gechōng* (革葱) has leaves resembling those of *xiè* (薤), but they are thicker.
Regarding *lánchōng* (蘭葱),
tradition states that it grows in the regions south of the Ling Mountains.
Its leaves resemble those of garlic but are broader, and its odor is like that of garlic. As for hiṅgu,
in the language of the Brahmins, the word *hiṅgu* refers to mustard.
I suspect that various monasteries in the Western Regions do not permit the consumption [of garlic].
It is also said that *hing-ju* (asafoetida) grows in the region south of the Five Ridges.
Its shape resembles that of Japanese leeks (*Allium ascalonicum*), and its flavor resembles garlic.
If there is a disease that other medicines cannot cure,
one should perhaps administer it.
Just as the Venerable Śāriputra practiced according to the Vinaya,
a Bodhisattva should also follow this principle.
There is a separate scripture in one fascicle titled *The Five Pungent Herbs*.
There are five types of pungent roots,
each with five varieties, totaling twenty-five.
Furthermore, it is said:
Because he consumed pungent food,
he entered the Avīci hell in the eastern direction.
Those who washed the pungent food upstream and those who washed the clothing downstream likewise [fell into hell], and so forth.
These three precepts have no distinct characteristics apart from the inclusion of wholesome qualities;
they are subsumed under their meaning and are likewise contained within non-negligence regarding body, speech, and mind.

5. The Fifth Precept on Exposing Faults and Teaching Repentance: If a disciple of the Buddha sees any sentient being violate the eight precepts, the five precepts, or the ten precepts; or commit breaches of prohibitions, the seven heinous acts, the eight difficulties, or any other offenses against the precepts—they ought to teach them to repent. Yet, if a Bodhisattva does not teach them to repent, but instead dwells with them, shares in the community’s offerings and benefits, and participates in the *poṣadha* along with the assembly for the recitation of the precepts, failing to expose their faults or instruct them in the correction of their transgressions, they commit a secondary offense (light defilement). To see a transgression and fail to teach repentance violates the principle of mutual benefit.
Even for a śrāvaka who protects themselves, this would not be permitted;
how much less so for a mahāsattva?
According to what appears in the *Prakaraṇābhidharma*, it seems to belong among the precepts for benefiting sentient beings.
Toward those who have committed transgressions,
one harbors within a sense of intimacy, the intention to benefit and bring them peace and happiness, and through this superior resolve,
subjects them to discipline, reprimand, punishment, or expulsion.
This is because he desires to cause them to emerge from unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states; yet,
in doing so, the Bodhisattva’s teaching and transforming of sentient beings is itself the fulfillment of his own Buddha-dharma.
Therefore, this precept is also included within the "precept of gathering wholesome qualities" (*kuśalasaṃgrāhaka-śīla*).
It involves the thorough and precise recognition of one's own transgressions;
thus, it is also contained within the "precept of deeply seeing faults" (*doṣadarśana-śīla*).
Although there is a distinction between oneself and others,
because the recognition of one's faults and the subsequent regret and removal thereof are the same, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna systems prohibit [such actions];
thus, both members of the two monastic orders incur a full offense.
The same principle applies to the other three assemblies as well as to laypeople.
The eight precepts and the five precepts are the lay precepts;
the ten precepts are the ten precepts for śrāmaṇeras.
"Violating the prohibitions" refers to the precepts of the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
Furthermore, the "ten precepts" refers to the ten major offenses;
"violating the prohibitions" refers to the forty-eight minor defilements.
The seven heinous offenses are as explained below.
Regarding the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), some say they are the eight grave offenses (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*); others say:
Regarding the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties:
since these eight difficulties are summoned by the commission of transgressions,
the result is spoken of within the context of the cause.
Now, among the thirteen difficulties, excluding those of the hermaphrodite, the eunuch, animals, non-humans, and those who have violated the two paths,
the remainder are called the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*).
Since the four [categories] beginning with the hermaphrodite are obstacles of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*), they possess no possibility of being removed through repentance.
Regarding those who have abandoned the two paths:
because they were in a different path and have returned to the Buddha-dharma,
there is no sense of living together or sharing in the same offerings.
For this reason, these five do not enter into the reckoning of the ritual confession (jiao-chan).
Within the forty-four [precepts], the seventh precept states:
"If a bodhisattva, toward sentient beings who are violent, malevolent, and violators of the precepts..."
With a mind harboring resentment and a mind filled with malice,
on account of that person’s violence and violation of precepts,
one employs means to abandon them and fails to provide benefit.
This is called an offense;
it is a defiled transgression if one abandons [the practice] due to indolence or laziness.
If one fails to provide benefit due to forgetfulness,
this is called an offense;
it is a transgression that is non-afflicted.
Why is this? It is not that Bodhisattvas give rise to a mind of compassion toward those sentient beings who maintain pure ethical discipline and whose physical, verbal,
and mental actions are practiced in tranquility, nor do they wish to benefit them.
There is no offense in the case of a violent and immoral sentient being who manifests in various causes of suffering;
that is to say, when the mind is deranged.
Or, desiring to employ skillful means to discipline and subdue them—
as explained in detail previously—
or for the sake of protecting the minds of many sentient beings.
Or, if one sets aside [the practice] through skillful means to protect the monastic regulations and does not provide benefit, there is no transgression in either case. 6.

The Sixth Precept: Providing for the Teacher and Requesting the Dharma. If a child of the Buddha sees a Mahāyāna Dharma Master, a fellow student of the Mahāyāna, or those with the same views and practices entering a monastery, a private residence, a city, or a town;
If anyone comes from a hundred or a thousand *li* away,
one should immediately rise to welcome them, see them off,
prostrate before them, and make offerings.
He made offerings three times every day,
providing the Dharma Master with daily food consisting of three *liang* of gold and a hundred-flavored meal,
as well as beds, seats, and medical supplies.
He provided everything that was required to them in full.
He constantly invited the Dharma Master to preach the Dharma during the three periods of the day,
and he paid homage three times every day.
One should not give rise to thoughts of anger or affliction;
for the sake of the Dharma, one should sacrifice the body and seek the Dharma without weariness.
If one does not do so,
one commits a minor offense (light impurity). This precept was established because by failing to request the Dharma when encountering others,
one loses the benefit of purifying the spirit.
If there are śrāvakas who know the methods for the detailed and abbreviated *poṣadha*,
they should be appointed to provide the necessary services.
Within five years, or as long as one has not mastered the five dharmas, one should request instruction from others.
If one does not [act accordingly], one commits an offense of the seventh category.
Beyond this, no further rules are established,
because it is easy to fulfill through self-restraint.
When a bodhisattva sees those who possess knowledge, they should always provide for them and invite them;
because their desire for what is wholesome is insatiable, all seven classes of followers commit the same offense [if they fail to do so].
In the preface to the text, there are two parts:
first, making offerings to the teacher; second, requesting the Dharma. There are two ways of making offerings to the teacher.
First, the offering of circumambulation;
second, the offering of food and drink;
and third, the offering performed three times each day.

This refers to the three periods within the day, or even during non-designated times when one may obtain non-designated beverages and the like as offerings. As for the phrase "eating three *liang* of gold daily": [it means that even if one were to consume such wealth, it would not constitute a violation].
This is said with reference to those who are capable of discernment;
or it is stated thus so as to cause them to revere the Dharma,
just as the man of the Snowy Mountains sacrificed his own life for the sake of a single verse.
How much more so with external wealth.
Third is the offering of service and attendance,
which means providing everything else that is required.
Regarding the request for the Dharma at the three times during the day:
this refers to morning, midday, and evening.
"Not giving rise to a mind of anger or a mind of resentment" means...
Even if the Dharma Master should act contrary to his wishes, one must never give rise to a mind of anger.
Although one may experience physical exhaustion from providing for him, one must not give rise to a mind of resentment or distress.
This is because one is willing to sacrifice one's body for the sake of the Dharma and to request the Dharma.
This explains the reason why one should not give rise to anger or affliction.
Should there be obstacles such as illness or hindrances,
or if the Dharma Master encounters impediments, [one should remain patient].
If one knows that the other is inferior and oneself is superior, there is no offense in not requesting instruction in this manner.

7. Listening to the Dharma and Consulting on Receiving Precepts. Seventh: Listening to the Dharma and Consulting on Receiving Precepts. If a disciple of the Buddha sees anywhere where the Dharma, Vinaya, Sutras, or Vinaya-pitaka are being expounded—whether in a great residence or a dwelling where the Dharma is being taught—a newly initiated Bodhisattva should take the volumes of the Sutras and Vinaya to the place of the Dharma Master to listen, receive, and inquire about them. Whether it be in mountain forests, under trees, in monastic grounds, or in any place where the Dharma is preached, they must go to all such places to listen, receive, and inquire. If they do not go to those places to listen, receive, and inquire, they commit a minor offense (light defilement). To see the teaching being given and not listen is an offense.
The regulations were established because mourning obstructs the path of advancing toward goodness.
The rules regarding similarities and differences in training are as previously stated.
Among the twenty-eight minor precepts, the eighth states:
If there is a place where the Dharma is being expounded within a distance of forty *li* from an upāsaka,
and he is unable to go and listen, he incurs an offense of negligence (*āpatti*).
In this context, "expounding the Dharma" refers to the exposition of the Vinaya-piṭaka, the Sūtras, and the Vinaya.
That which elucidates the Dharma is called Sūtra;
that which elucidates the Vinaya is called Vinaya;
the remaining texts are easy to understand.
The thirty-second precept among the forty-four states: "If a bodhisattva,
upon hearing that the sublime Dharma is being taught or that there is a formal discussion for its definitive discernment,
fails to go and listen because they are constrained by pride, harboring a mind of resentment or a mind of malice."
This is called an offense;
it is a defiled transgression if one fails to go and listen due to being overcome by indolence and laziness.
This is not a defiled offense.
There is no offense if one was unaware.
If one has a disease,
or lacks physical strength,
or knows that one is speaking erroneously.
If one protects the mind of that speaker of the Dharma,
and correctly understands the meaning of what is spoken—
having heard it repeatedly, retained it, and comprehended it.
If one has already become widely learned, being fully endowed with the power of hearing and retention,
and has accumulated that learning,
yet wishes to dwell the mind upon an object without further reliance on hearing;
If one diligently cultivates the superior meditative concentrations of a bodhisattva,
yet recognizes oneself to be of the highest degree of dullness and that one's wisdom is blunted and turbid,
making it difficult to receive and retain the teachings one has heard.
There is no transgression if one does not go to listen because it is difficult to collect the mind on the object of focus and achieve meditative concentration.

8. The Eighth Precept: Not Turning One’s Back on the Mahāyāna. If a disciple of the Buddha turns their heart away from the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas that abide eternally, claiming they were not spoken by the Buddha, and instead accepts and upholds the precepts of the two vehicles, the evil views of external paths, or all those sūtras and vinayas of false views, they commit a light offense (light impurity). This is established because [such an act] abandons the root for the sake of the branches and deviates from what one has studied.
The Śrāvakas do not establish prohibitions because their respective trainings differ;
[the precepts] are common to all seven classes of followers.
Regarding the passage in the text where those who turn their backs on the Mahāyāna claim that the *Nitya-sūtra* and *Vinaya* were not spoken by the Buddha:
the old commentary states that this was intended solely to restrain indecision and resolve uncertainty.
This is the expedient means of inferior, false views.
If one definitively asserts that the Great [Vehicle] is inferior and the Small [Vehicle] is superior,
one will lose the precepts as a result of such reckoning.
If, in one's heart, one desires to turn away from [the teachings], claiming they are not the true teaching,
and intends to accept the sutras and vinaya of the two vehicles or external paths,
one commits this minor defilement even before the plan has been carried out.
However, even if the schemes of superior or middling wrong views have not yet been accomplished, one commits a minor offense;
this is governed by the same preceptual restriction.
Here, for the sake of discussion, we cite the case of turning one's back on the Great [Vehicle] and inclining toward the Lesser.
Because ordinary beings and bodhisattvas frequently engage in these matters, if they were to express them in words,
there would be two types. If one speaks with the notion that "dharmas" exist,
then even if the precepts and virtues have already passed away, [the conceptualization remains].
If one speaks with the perception that it is not the Dharma, one commits the tenth grave offense.
Now, it is said that if one’s mind is opposed to the Mahāyāna while upholding the Śrāvaka vehicle,
even if one gives rise to the perception that it is the Dharma, one does not necessarily lose the precepts.
This refers, for example, to someone who, although having generated the great resolve and received the bodhisattva precepts,
has never studied the profound Mahāyāna sūtras,
but has only heard that one attains the fruit beneath the tree after practicing the Hīnayāna for three kalpas.
When suddenly hearing the profound meaning of the Mahāyāna,
their minds do not give rise to faith and they claim it was not spoken by the Buddha;
yet, because they do not regress from the great resolve, they do not lose their precepts.
Because one forms the notion that it is a [mere] phenomenon, one does not commit a grave offense.
Therefore, the twenty-ninth of the forty-four precepts in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:

"If a bodhisattva conceals the most profound and supreme profundity of the true meaning of the Dharma, or the inconceivable spiritual power of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, at a place where they are hidden..."
They do not give rise to faith or understanding;
they harbor resentment, turn their backs on it, and slander it; it does not lead to the ultimate goal, nor does it lead to the Dharma;
it was not spoken by the Tathāgata.
If one is unable to benefit and bring peace and happiness to sentient beings,
this is called an offense;
such a transgression constitutes a defiled violation.
Such slander arises either from one's own internal improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*),
or from conforming to others by making such a statement; that is,
when hearing about the profound and most profound points, the mind lacks faith and understanding.
At that time, the bodhisattva should resolutely believe and accept it;
they should be free from deceit and crookedness,
and should train themselves in this way.
I have acted unskillfully;
blind and lacking the eye of wisdom,
I have followed whatever was proclaimed by the Tathāgata’s own eye.
They give rise to slander regarding the intentional language of the Tathāgatas.
Thus, the bodhisattva, remaining in ignorance, looks upward and defers to the Tathāgata, [thinking],
"There is nothing among the Buddha-dharmas that the Tathāgata does not directly know."
They observe and contemplate accordingly;
thus practicing correctly, they do not commit any transgression.
Although they lack faith and understanding, they do not engage in disparagement.
Regarding the phrase "the two vehicles, śrāvakas, and those with the evil views of external paths":
the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas are termed the "two vehicles and śrāvakas.
These very śrāvakas are outside of the Mahāyāna.
Because they deviate from the bodhisattva path, they are called the evil views of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Furthermore, the six teachers and others are termed non-Buddhist evil views.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
If bodhisattvas transgress the bodhisattva dharma and investigate the treatises of heterodox paths and various non-Buddhist systems, becoming skillful in them,
cherishing them with a deep mind, and becoming attached to their flavor.
It is not like the case of medicinal pungent herbs, which one may habitually approach;
this is called an offense.
This constitutes a transgression of defiled violation, the twenty-eighth.
The opening conditions up to the twenty-fourth [chapter] shall be explained later.

These three precepts above are precisely what is taught in the *Śīlaparivarta* (Chapter on Ethics) of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* as the diligent cultivation and study of hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*) within the "precept for gathering wholesome qualities" (*kuśaladharmasaṃgrāhaka-śīla*).

**The Ninth Precept on Attending to the Sick** If a Buddha’s disciple sees anyone who is ill, they should always provide for them with offerings no different from those given to the Buddha. Among the eight fields of merit, the field of merit consisting of attending to the sick is the foremost. If parents, teachers, monks, or disciples fall ill—with their various faculties impaired and suffering from a hundred kinds of ailments—one must provide for them all so that they may recover. If a Bodhisattva, out of a heart of anger or resentment, fails to attend to them, or even if they see someone sick in a monastery, a city, a wilderness, a mountain forest, or on a road and do not provide relief, they commit a secondary offense (light impurity). This precept is established because failing to rescue others in their suffering violates the practice of cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Śrāvakas abide by the Dharma;
this applies to those who share the same Dharma with their teachers and friends, as well as those appointed by the Saṃgha.
Beyond these, no further restrictions are prescribed.
Because his original vow was not to assist others,
the Great Being should save all;
because his original aspiration was to universally embrace them.

This is a regulation common to all seven assemblies of the Sangha; it refers to the practice described in the treatise of providing compassionate, earnest, and reverent nursing and offerings for those who are ill.
As the text states: "One should provide for all persons with illnesses as one would for the Buddha, without distinction."
The Buddha is the ultimate object of reverence;
illness is the ultimate object of compassion. Although reverence and compassion differ, [they are both essential].
The meaning of "field" (*kṣetra*) is the same as before, and thus there is no difference.
Among the eight fields of merit, the field of merit of nursing the sick is the foremost.
This is because it first involves the compassionate mind that seeks to save others, whereas the other fields primarily involve the sense of reverence and honor.
Although there are eight types of fields of merit, nursing the sick is supreme.
If one provides care for parents or teachers until they recover, this is considered the highest,
even though it was mentioned only in general terms.
All are to be saved, from the closest kin to the most distant, without any lack of priority;
therefore, it specifically mentions one's own relatives.
Regarding the second precept among the eleven matters for benefiting sentient beings in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages), it says:
If a bodhisattva, upon seeing sentient beings afflicted by a grave illness,
fails to go and attend to them out of a mind of resentment or a mind of malice,
this is called an offense.
To transgress in this way constitutes a defiled offense; however,
if one fails to go and provide service due to being overcome by indolence or laziness,
it is a non-defiled offense.
There is no transgression if one is personally ill,
or if one lacks physical strength.
If one requests another who is capable and compliant to go and attend to them;
or if one knows that the patient has someone to rely upon and protect them;
or if one knows that the patient themselves possesses the strength to attend to their own needs.
If one understands that one is capable of sustaining oneself when afflicted by long-term illness;
or if one intends to diligently cultivate vast, unsurpassed, and sublime wholesome qualities;
or if one desires to protect and maintain the wholesome qualities already cultivated so that they remain uninterrupted.
If one knows for oneself that one is of the highest degree of dullness and stupidity,
such that one's wisdom is dull and turbid, making it difficult to receive and retain the teachings heard,
and difficult to collect the mind upon an object of focus to bring it to meditative concentration;
If one has previously promised another to perform an act of worship,
such as acting as a companion for the sick or for those in pain.
If one wishes to eliminate their suffering, one should know that it is likewise so. **The Tenth Precept:

Not Keeping Instruments of Killing** If a Buddha’s disciple does not keep any swords, staves, bows, arrows, spears, axes, or implements for battle, nor any evil nets, snares, or traps—any instruments for killing living beings—they must not keep any of these. Yet, even if a Bodhisattva were to kill their own parents, they would still not seek retribution; how much less would they kill any other sentient being? If one intentionally keeps swords or staves, they commit a minor offense (light defilement). When views and afflictions are fully present, the practice of the matter is not without gradual habituation.
It was established as a prohibition for the sake of profound protection;
that is, it constitutes the correct practice of guarding the various training rules (*śikṣāpada*),
wherein the avoidance of unwholesome deeds implies the inclusion of wholesome ones.
Both large and small [precepts] are equally prohibited, and both monastics and laypeople are forbidden [from possessing them].
However, if it is a person of high status, such as a king or a prince, who wishes to prevent external threats by preparing bows, arrows, and the like, then in principle it should be permitted.
One must simply not go so far as to cause injury.
Furthermore, even if one is not a person of high status, if one wishes to protect the Dharma,
one may prepare weapons.
Those whose minds are free from harmful intent should also be permitted [to carry weapons].
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is stated that laypeople are allowed to carry staves and weapons for the sake of protecting the Dharma.
One must simply not go so far as to kill.
The commentary on this passage is easy to understand.

These ten precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent mind; they will be explained in detail in the following six chapters. The section beginning with "Thus" concludes by exhorting one to uphold them.
The "lower six chapters" refers to the expanded version.
Alternatively, as some scriptures state "six sets of six chapters," there must have been a separate set of six sets of six chapters.

2. Regarding the Ten Precepts: within the twentieth precept, the first four precepts subsume the goodness of one's own practice (*sva-caryā-kuśala*), while the latter six subsume the goodness of transforming others (*para-caryā-kuśala*).
Among the first four:

1. The First Precept: Not Serving as a Messenger for a State. The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha, one must not, for the sake of profit or out of an evil mind, serve as a messenger for a state to convey orders for military arrays, the mobilization of armies, or mutual attacks that slaughter immeasurable sentient beings. A Bodhisattva may not even enter an army to come and go there, much less intentionally act as a traitor to a state. If one does so intentionally, one commits a secondary offense (light defilement). Now, regarding serving as a messenger for a state:..."
If one necessarily harbors expectations of victory or defeat within their emotions,
employing deceitful stratagems to compel others to battle,
they internally violate the principle of universal compassion.
Because it externally harms the lives of sentient beings,
its cessation is prescribed.
This is regulated by both the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna.
This precept is prohibited for all seven classes of followers.
Regarding the inclusion of "virtue" (*śīla*) within the discussion of gathering wholesome qualities, those who abide in non-negligence of body, speech,
and mind also include this precept within the aggregates (*skandha*).
To harbor an evil mind for the sake of profit is mental negligence;
to issue commands and dispatch messengers is verbal negligence;
and to move back and forth within the army is physical negligence.
Regarding the statement "due to an evil mind for the sake of gain and offerings":
because the mind intends to enrich oneself, it is an evil mind;
because it seeks to harm others for the sake of profit, it is an evil mind.
If it is for the purpose of reconciling relations between this and that,
such activities are not prohibited by the principles of the household life;
this applies to those who serve as envoys throughout the realm.
This refers to acting as a messenger between two kingdoms.
"The meeting of military arrays" refers to the two kingdoms engaging in combat.
As for the immeasurable sentient beings who were killed as armies raised against one another, this grave matter was brought about by me acting as a messenger.
"Raising armies" means to mobilize; "armies" refers to the multitudes of soldiers.
If one intends to cause a killing,
one incurs a grave offense (pārājika) as soon as the preceding life is severed; however,
in the present case, because one merely restrains the messenger, one incurs a light offense of impurity (duṣkṛta).
One must not enter or travel within military encampments;
battlefields are chaotic and mixed, and are places not trodden by those on the Way.
Unless there is an urgent necessity, both monastics and laypeople are strictly forbidden from entering.
If a lay bodhisattva is appointed as a military official and his reputation for valor and majesty is such that he cannot avoid [the duty], he may,
for the sake of pacifying the nation, allow himself to enter [the fray];
however, he must not cause harm.
It was as when the Śākya clan fought with the Vaiśālī Licchavis.
If there is a cause or condition for a renunciant bodhisattva to be summoned,
according to the Vinaya, they should be permitted to stay for two or three nights.

**The Second Precept on Not Engaging in Evil Trade** If a disciple of the Buddha intentionally engages in the trade of free persons, slaves, or domestic animals; or in the commerce of coffins, wooden planks, or other implements used for containing the dead, they should not do so themselves, much less teach others to do so. If one intentionally does so oneself or teaches others to do so, one commits a secondary offense (light defilement). This constitutes the sin of harming the environment while coveting profit.
Because the harm and affliction involved are profound, it is established as a prohibition.
It is prescribed equally for both the great and the small [vehicles], and is not common to the seven classes of followers.
If one sells items that cause harm to sentient beings, such as selling living creatures,
it is forbidden for both monastics and laypeople alike.
If one sells items for the sake of profit, such as the mutual exchange of cloth and silk, it is likewise prohibited.
To regulate the Path and open up for the secular world, the *Upāsaka-sūtra* states:
"A layperson who acquires wealth should divide it into four parts."
One part is used for making offerings to one's parents, wife, and children;
two parts are used for trade in accordance with the Dharma;
and the remaining one part is set aside for accumulation and storage.
Now, this precept also prohibits negligence of body and speech.
Regarding the scriptural phrase "one who sells a free person":
it refers to one who knows that the person does not belong to themselves.
Furthermore, those who engage in forceful or fraudulent buying and selling of slaves and livestock—
though these items belong to them— [commit an offense].
There may be instances where one incurs an offense by causing division or by encroaching upon and damaging [the property].
Regarding the trade of coffin planks and wood— the implements used for containing the dead—
the coffin itself is composed of these planks and wood.
"Or wooden boards" refers to the outer coffin and other such wooden structures.
Since one does not even do this intentionally, how much less would one teach others to do so?
In this context, the author cites his own case as an illustration for others.
Regarding the precept against drinking alcohol, because it involves self-indulgence and negligence, one uses others as an illustration for oneself;
regarding this precept against selling, because it involves harming the interests of others, one uses oneself as an illustration for others.
This is the intended meaning behind these mutual comparisons between self and others.

3. The Third Precept: Not Slandering the Virtuous and Good. If a disciple of the Buddha, out of a malicious mind, slanders others who are virtuous and good—such as Dharma masters, teachers, monks, kings, or nobles—without cause, saying they have committed the seven reversals or the ten grave offenses; or if, toward their parents, siblings, and six kinds of relatives, they ought to give rise to hearts of filial piety and compassion, yet instead further increase their rebellious harm so that these people fall into undesirable states, this constitutes a transgression of a minor defilement offense. This precept is established to prohibit the groundless slander and entrapment of virtuous persons.
This precept is regulated by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles and is forbidden to all seven classes of practitioners;
it specifically restrains verbal negligence.
Question: Since this precept prohibits the grave offense of slandering others, what is the difference between it and the sixth grave offense?

Answer: In order to distinguish the characteristics of these two precepts, the masters of old have formulated four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) each for cases involving a basis (*sādhāraṇa*) and cases lacking a basis (*asādhāraṇa*).
Regarding the four propositions concerning those who possess the roots:
one who possesses the precepts speaks of both grave and minor offenses for a person who possesses the precepts.
All minor defilements are transgressions;
this precept specifically prohibits [interacting] with those who lack the precepts.
Regarding those who have no precepts, both grave offenses and minor offenses constitute a transgression of the light defilement;
this is governed by the preceding precept.
Third, to speak of the grave and light offenses of those who lack precepts to those who possess precepts is also a transgression of a minor stain.
This precept also governs those who have entered the four stages of the path and those who lack the precepts,
regarding the speaking of faults against those who possess the precepts.
If one speaks of a grave offense, it is grave;
the preceding precept strictly prohibits this.
If one speaks of a minor transgression, it is minor.
The preceding precept governs both cases.
Regarding the four permutations concerning the groundless [accusation]:
it applies exclusively to one who possesses the precepts.
It is stated that for one who possesses the precepts, both grave offenses and minor offenses are all considered light defilements;
this precept is found in the text.
The first [set of] three phrases prescribe heavy offenses for intentional acts and light offenses for those not so intended;
the latter three phrases follow the same ritual procedure as before,
differing only in that they concern groundless accusations.
Furthermore, some say that within the sixth section, speaking of actual faults is prohibited;
they claim this is because it involves speaking of the transgressions of the fourfold assembly.
In this present precept, groundless slander is prohibited,
as the text states that one slanders another who is virtuous and good; however,
in the preceding and succeeding two precepts, there is still no distinction made regarding the person to whom the accusation is addressed.
Since there is no distinction made between those who possess the precepts and those who do not, it stands to reason that [the offense] applies to both.
Question: In the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, there is no grave offense for groundless slander.
It is said that [otherwise] one would actually commit a minor offense.
Why, then, does the Bodhisattva act contrary to this?
The answer is: within the Śrāvaka-dharma, the precepts are established to guard against one's own transgressions.
Groundless slander of others involves a grave fault of intention;
speaking of faults based on grounds may involve a lighter fault of intention.
Therefore, there is a difference in the gravity of the prohibitions.
Within the Bodhisattva Dharma, it is prescribed that one must protect others from harm.
To speak of another's actual transgressions may result in permanent injury and cause them to fall back or sink.
Since a groundless accusation is not factual,
it cannot cause permanent harm;
this is the principle underlying the distinction between grave and light offenses.
Regarding the phrase "with an evil mind and without cause," it is called an "evil mind" because one solely desires to disparage another with no intention of providing benefit.
It is called "without cause" because the three roots [of unwholesome action] arise without any basis.
A "good person" (*liáng-rén*) is one who is slandered by others yet truly has committed no transgression; thus they are called "good and virtuous.
They are called "good" (*liáng*) because their perception is pure, and they are called "virtuous" (*shàn*) because their reality is pure.
This is not like the previous precept where one who is not a slave is called "good.
The mention of the Dharma Master, the Preceptor, the King,
and persons of noble rank specifically cites those among the objects of slander that constitute grave offenses.
Regarding the mention of committing the seven inversions and ten grave offenses,
this specifically cites those that are most serious among the acts of slander.
As for "parents, brothers, and the six types of relatives," [this refers to those within one's kin].
Since the three periods of time are mutually integrated and nothing is not one's own kin,
to instead commit further acts of rebellion and harm against them is a grave slander; thus it is said that "rebellion is added."
Regarding "falling into an undesirable state":
it is because of my slandering that one falls into a state contrary to one's wishes. **The Fourth Precept:

Not to Light Fires Unawares** If a Buddha’s disciple, out of an evil mind, sets a great fire to burn mountains, forests, or wildernesses from the fourth month until the ninth month; or if they set fire to others’ houses, dwellings, cities, monasteries, fields, trees, or the property of spirits, officials, or any other owned objects—they must not intentionally burn them. If one intentionally burns them, they commit a minor offense (light defilement). To light fires indiscriminately, regardless of time or place, results in much actual injury and damage.
Therefore, it is established as a prohibition.
Both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna prohibit it.
Among the seven classes of followers, for the five monastic groups, it is entirely prohibited at all times.

Regarding the location, it was prohibited to be in the open but permitted to be covered for the two groups of householders; regarding the time, it was prohibited during the heat but permitted during the cold because of the necessity of their livelihoods;
thus, both being in the open and being covered were permitted in those circumstances.
However, one must not allow the vines to grow and cause damage.
Inferring the meaning of this precept,

One does not share a state with those who have killed one's brother.

Internally integrating the three periods of time, one realizes that enemies and kin are of a single thread;
how, then, could one permit the killing of this relative for the sake of that relative?
Therefore, even if one kills a father or elder brother, one must not seek retribution.
Furthermore, once my own kinsman has died, they cannot be restored to life;
even if I were to harm that kinsman, what benefit would it bring me?
Thus, the *Lāngshòuwáng jīng* (The Sūtra of King Dīrghāyu) says:
To repay enmity with enmity,
the enmity will never cease;
to repay enmity with virtue— this brings it to an end.
Only then will enmity be extinguished.
Even if the sovereign of a state is killed by another, one must not seek retribution;
this refers to cases where the sovereign has killed one's own kin for the sake of another.
Furthermore, one must not seek retribution against the sovereign of the state,
for the sovereign is likewise a kinsman.
Moreover, it may happen that my own sovereign is killed by an enemy state.
Nor should one seek retribution against another country,
for that too is kin; this is precisely what is meant by the "Everlasting Sword of Peace."
Regarding the claim that taking life to repay one's birth is contrary to the way of filial piety:
this is because even an enemy was once a relative, and thus also possesses the kindness of having given one life.
Therefore, by taking that person's life, one repays the kindness of one's own birth.
This is not filial piety; it is contrary to the Way.
This would constitute a grave offense distinct from the timing of the killing;

If one does not even keep [the aforementioned offenses],
